content: Self-harm, defined as intentional self-poisoning or self-injury, is a prevalent issue among children and adolescents. It is often recurrent and strongly linked to suicide. This review focuses on psychosocial and pharmacological interventions specifically for self-harm in this population, updating and refining previous Cochrane reviews on the topic. The objective of this review was to identify all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated psychosocial interventions, pharmacological treatments, or natural products for self-harm in children and adolescents. The aim was to compare the effects of these treatments with standard care, placebo, or alternative treatments through meta-analyses where possible. The search for relevant studies was conducted using the Cochrane Depression, Anxiety, and Neurosis Group (CCDAN) Specialised Register, with the most recent search completed on January 30, 2015. The inclusion criteria were RCTs involving children and adolescents (up to 18 years old) who had engaged in self-harm within the previous six months and had presented to clinical services. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the evidence. For binary outcomes, odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% CI were used. Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model when data were available. A total of 11 trials involving 1,126 participants were included in the review. The majority of participants were female (mean = 80.6% across 10 trials reporting gender). All included trials evaluated psychosocial interventions; no trials of pharmacological treatments were identified. Most interventions were assessed in single trials, except for dialectical behavior therapy for adolescents (DBT-A) and group-based psychotherapy, which were evaluated in multiple trials. Therapeutic assessment was found to improve adherence to subsequent treatment compared to treatment as usual (TAU) in one trial (n = 70; OR = 5.12, 95% CI 1.70 to 15.39). However, this intervention did not significantly reduce the repetition of self-harm at 12 months (n = 69; OR = 0.75, 95% CI 0.18 to 3.06) or 24 months (n = 69; OR = 0.69, 95% CI 0.23 to 2.14). The evidence for this finding was of low quality, and the results were based on a single cluster-randomized trial, which may have overestimated the intervention's effectiveness. Mentalisation therapy was associated with a reduction in the number of adolescents scoring above the cut-off for repeated self-harm on the Risk-Taking and Self-Harm Inventory at 12 months post-intervention (n = 71; OR = 0.26, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.78). This evidence was of moderate quality and suggests potential benefits for adolescents with multiple episodes of self-harm or emerging personality problems. DBT-A did not significantly reduce the proportion of adolescents repeating self-harm compared to TAU or enhanced usual care (n = 104; OR = 0.72, 95% CI 0.12 to 4.40). However, one trial reported that adolescents in the DBT-A group experienced a greater reduction in the frequency of repeated self-harm over time, as well as significant improvements in depression, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation. Group-based psychotherapy showed no significant effect on reducing self-harm repetition at six months (n = 430; OR = 1.72, 95% CI 0.56 to 5.24) or 12 months (n = 490; OR = 0.80, 95% CI 0.22 to 2.97). The evidence for these findings was of low quality, and there was considerable heterogeneity between studies (I² = 65% and 77%, respectively). Other interventions, including compliance enhancement, CBT-based psychotherapy, home-based family intervention, and provision of an emergency card, did not demonstrate significant effects on reducing self-harm repetition compared to TAU. The quality of evidence for these interventions ranged from very low to low. No data were reported on adverse effects beyond the planned outcomes related to suicidal behavior. In conclusion, there is limited evidence to support the effectiveness of interventions for self-harm in children and adolescents. Most findings were based on single trials, and the quality of evidence was generally low or very low. While therapeutic assessment, mentalisation therapy, and DBT-A show some promise, further research is needed to evaluate these approaches. Large-scale trials with standardized outcome measures, including adverse events, are required. Additionally, the development of new interventions should involve collaboration with patients to ensure their relevance and effectiveness.
